title: Simran while working
hookLine: the Name can run quietly underneath ordinary work
carry: hands at work, heart at home
last: BREATH · WAHEGURU · SATNAM · COME BACK · AMRIT VELA · MALA.

cards: You can't sit with your eyes closed all day. There's a job. There are kids, a commute, a sink full of dishes, a shift that starts at seven.

If remembering God only happens in the quiet corner before dawn, most of the day is left out. The Sikh Gurus were never monks. They farmed, traded, married and ran communities, so they had to answer this.
Their answer is in a small, funny conversation between two saints.

teach.b: Among the short verses of Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib, there's an exchange between two earlier saints of India, Trilochan and Namdev. Namdev was a cloth printer by trade, working with dyes all day.
Trilochan teases him, in paraphrase: Namdev, you've been caught by the world. Why are you busy printing calico? Why not fix your mind on the Lord?

teach.h: HANDS AND FEET DO THE WORK.
teach.b: Namdev answers, in paraphrase: with your mouth, keep the Lord's Name; with your hands and feet, do all your work; keep your consciousness with the Immaculate One. The work doesn't stop. The remembering doesn't stop.
One runs underneath the other, like a song you hum while you cook. That fits the whole Sikh way of life.
You've met the three pillars Sikhs trace to Guru Nanak: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn an honest living; vand chhako, share.
They sit side by side. For Sikhs, honest work isn't a distraction from the spiritual life. It's part of it.
So what does it look like? For some, a quiet Waheguru under the breath while stacking shelves or driving.
For others, a recording of kirtan playing while they work, or a single breath of remembering each time a task begins or ends.

teach.h: HANDS AT WORK, HEART AT HOME.
teach.b: The hymns hold up remembering with every breath; in a working day, it's more like a home the heart can return to all day, while the hands stay busy.

how: Many Sikhs keep up simran through the working day, quietly repeating Waheguru, listening to kirtan while they work, or pausing for a breath of remembering between tasks.

o: remembering the Name, even beneath daily work
a prayer said only inside the gurdwara
a silent retreat away from daily life

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: why are you busy printing cloth?
hands and feet do all the work

s: Sikhs see work as a distraction from spiritual life
honest work, kirat karo, is one of the three pillars, alongside remembering and sharing.
the Namdev and Trilochan exchange is in the Guru Granth Sahib
it's among the saloks of Kabir, near the end of the Granth.
Namdev gave up his trade to meditate
in the verse he keeps working: the hands work, the consciousness stays with the Lord.

games.q: you're Namdev, dyeing cloth, and a friend teases you: why not stop and fix your mind on God? what do you say?
o: you're right, I'll close the shop.
let the hands work and the heart remember.
God can wait until the work is done.
games.why: Namdev's answer: with hands and feet do all your work, and keep your consciousness with the Immaculate One.

practice: Stand up if you can and walk slowly, around the room, down a hallway or in place, letting each step land with a word: left foot, Wahe; right foot, Guru; or, if you'd rather, left foot, in-breath; right foot, out.
Keep your eyes open: you're still in the world, doing something ordinary, with the remembering running underneath. When the mind wanders, come back.

wordCard.voice: Simran. The Name running quietly underneath ordinary work, as Namdev said: hands and feet at work, the heart with the One.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: simran, remembering, the practice this week has been about.

carryVoice: Your line: hands at work, heart at home. The dye and the Name, together, all day long. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Kabir 212–213, Ang 1375–1376 (Trilochan and Namdev)
